short: The study of the whole economy: total output, jobs, inflation, interest rates and trade, rather than single firms or households.
kid: Instead of looking at one lemonade stand, we look at the whole town. Is everyone busy, are things costing more, and is the town making more than last year?
detail: Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole: gross domestic product, inflation, unemployment, interest rates, exchange rates, government budgets and the balance of payments. Microeconomics, by contrast, looks at individual consumers, firms and markets. Macro asks why economies grow, why they fall into recessions and how central banks and governments respond through monetary and fiscal policy. For investors it sets the backdrop: growth drives corporate earnings, inflation and policy rates drive bond yields and valuations, and the exchange rate shapes foreign flows. In India, the big releases include quarterly GDP and monthly CPI inflation from the National Statistics Office, and the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee decisions, which under the rules as of 2025 come at least four times a year (six in practice). A common confusion is expecting macro data to predict daily stock prices: markets react to the surprise versus expectations, not the level alone.
example: Say an economy's output, measured at constant prices, rises from ₹200 lakh crore to ₹214 lakh crore while consumer prices rise 4% and unemployment holds at 5%. A macro analyst sums this up as 7% real growth (14 / 200) with moderate inflation, a mix that usually supports company profits.

short: The total value of all final goods and services produced inside a country in a period, usually a quarter or a year.
kid: Imagine adding up every toy, cake and haircut made in your whole country in one year. That big total shows how busy everyone has been.
detail: Gross domestic product measures everything produced within a country's borders, whoever owns the factory. It can be calculated three ways that should agree: the expenditure method (consumption + investment + government spending + net exports), the income method (wages, profits, rent and interest) and the production method (value added by each sector). Only final goods count, so the steel in a car is not counted twice. Headlines usually quote real GDP growth, which strips out price changes. India's National Statistics Office releases quarterly estimates about two months after each quarter ends, followed by several revisions. For investors, GDP growth drives corporate earnings, tax collections and policy decisions. Common confusions: GDP measures output, not wealth or well-being, and a large total says little about how income is shared; GDP per capita is better for comparing living standards.
example: Say an economy has consumption of ₹180 lakh crore, investment of ₹100 lakh crore, government spending of ₹35 lakh crore, exports of ₹65 lakh crore and imports of ₹80 lakh crore. GDP = 180 + 100 + 35 + (65 - 80) = ₹300 lakh crore.
formula: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M)

short: The value of what an economy produces minus the cost of the inputs used up to make it, measured sector by sector.
kid: A baker buys flour and sells bread for more than the flour cost. The extra the bread is worth, beyond the flour, is what the baker added.
detail: Gross value added measures what each producer adds: the value of its output minus intermediate consumption, meaning raw materials, energy and services bought from others. Summing GVA across agriculture, industry and services gives the economy's supply-side picture. GVA at basic prices plus taxes on products minus subsidies on products equals GDP at market prices. India has used GVA at basic prices for its sectoral estimates since the 2015 switch to the 2011-12 base year, and analysts often prefer it to judge underlying activity because GDP can be swung by changes in tax collections or subsidy payouts. For investors, sectoral GVA shows where growth is coming from, for instance whether manufacturing or financial services are leading. Common confusion: GVA growth and GDP growth can differ in a given quarter, sometimes by a percentage point, mainly because of net product taxes rather than real activity.
example: Say a hypothetical carmaker, ABC Motors Ltd, sells cars worth ₹1,000 crore and spends ₹700 crore on steel, parts and power bought from other firms. Its GVA is ₹300 crore. If an economy's GVA is ₹270 lakh crore, product taxes are ₹33 lakh crore and product subsidies are ₹3 lakh crore, GDP is 270 + 33 - 3 = ₹300 lakh crore.
formula: GVA = Value of output - Intermediate consumption; GDP = GVA at basic prices + Product taxes - Product subsidies

short: The value of everything an economy produces measured at current prices, so it rises with both more output and higher prices.
kid: If you sell the same ten cups of lemonade but ask for more coins per cup, your jar fills up more. This counts the fuller jar, even though you made no extra lemonade.
detail: Nominal GDP values output at the prices actually prevailing in each period, without adjusting for inflation. It therefore grows both when the economy produces more and when prices rise. Real GDP removes the price effect, and the gap between the two growth rates is roughly inflation as measured by the GDP deflator. Nominal GDP matters a lot in practice: company revenues, tax collections and wages are earned in nominal rupees, so nominal growth tracks top-line growth for listed firms better than real growth does. India's Union Budget sets fiscal deficit and debt targets as shares of nominal GDP and assumes a nominal growth rate when projecting revenue. A common confusion is reading high nominal growth as strong activity; when inflation is high, real growth may be weak. Conversely, very low inflation can slow nominal growth and hurt revenues and tax collections even when real growth is decent.
example: Say an economy's nominal GDP rises from ₹300 lakh crore to ₹330 lakh crore, growth of 10%. If prices across the economy rose 4%, real growth is 1.10 / 1.04 - 1 = about 5.8%, not 6%.
formula: Nominal GDP = Real GDP x GDP deflator / 100

short: The value of an economy's output measured at fixed base-year prices, so its growth shows the change in actual volume, not prices.
kid: Count how many cups of lemonade you made this year compared to last year. Asking for more coins per cup does not count, only making more cups does.
detail: Real GDP values each year's goods and services at the prices of a chosen base year, or the previous year in chain-linked systems, stripping out inflation. Real GDP growth is the headline growth figure because it shows whether the economy is actually producing more. Statisticians deflate each component separately; the GDP deflator is then derived as nominal divided by real GDP. For investors, real growth signals demand for goods, jobs and credit, while nominal growth drives revenues. India's national accounts are periodically re-based to a more recent year to reflect a changed economy, and a base change can revise past growth rates. Common confusion: a country can post very strong real growth from a low base after a slump, as India did after the 2020-21 contraction, so compare the level of output with its pre-shock trend as well.
example: Say nominal GDP is ₹330 lakh crore this year and the GDP deflator is 110 (base year = 100). Real GDP = 330 / 1.10 = ₹300 lakh crore. If real GDP was ₹280 lakh crore last year, real growth is 20 / 280 = about 7.1%.
formula: Real GDP = Nominal GDP / (GDP deflator / 100)

short: A price index covering everything an economy produces, found by dividing nominal GDP by real GDP and multiplying by 100.
kid: It tells you how much more all the town's toys and cakes cost now than in an earlier year. If the same things cost more, this number goes up.
detail: The GDP deflator measures the average price level of all final goods and services produced in an economy, relative to a base year. Unlike the Consumer Price Index, it does not use a fixed shopping basket: it covers investment goods, government services and exports, and excludes imports, so its weights shift with what the economy actually produces. Its annual change is the broadest measure of domestic inflation and is the link between nominal and real growth. In India the deflator has often tracked wholesale prices more closely than retail prices, because statisticians have used WPI to deflate much of goods output; when WPI inflation is very low, that can make real growth look stronger. Common confusion: a low or falling deflator does not mean shoppers are paying less; consumer prices can still be rising.
example: Say nominal GDP is ₹330 lakh crore and real GDP is ₹300 lakh crore. The deflator is 330 / 300 x 100 = 110. If it was 105 a year earlier, deflator inflation is 110 / 105 - 1 = about 4.8%.
formula: GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) x 100

short: A country's GDP divided by its population, giving the average output, and roughly the average income, per person.
kid: If a family bakes 20 cookies and there are 4 people, that is 5 cookies each. This number shows how much each person in a whole country gets, on average.
detail: GDP per capita divides total output by population and is the standard quick measure for comparing living standards across countries or over time. Comparisons are made either at market exchange rates or at purchasing power parity (PPP), which adjusts for lower prices in poorer countries; India's figure at PPP is several times its figure in dollars at market rates. A large economy can still be poor per person: India ranks among the biggest economies by total GDP but far lower per head. In Indian news, per capita income usually means per capita net national income from the National Statistics Office, which subtracts depreciation and net income paid abroad, so it differs from GDP per capita. Common confusion: it is an average, so it hides inequality; the typical (median) person can earn far less.
example: Say a country has GDP of $4 trillion and a population of 1.45 billion. GDP per capita = 4,000 billion / 1.45 billion = about $2,759. Another country with GDP of $0.5 trillion and 10 million people has GDP per capita of $50,000.
formula: GDP per capita = GDP / Population

short: The total income earned by a country's residents, at home or abroad: GDP plus income received from abroad minus income paid abroad.
kid: Count the cookies baked in your house, then add the cookies your sister earns helping at a friend's house. Take away the cookies you give the neighbour who helped in your kitchen.
detail: Gross national product, now usually called gross national income (GNI) in the UN System of National Accounts, measures income belonging to a country's residents wherever it is earned. It equals GDP plus net factor income from abroad: wages, interest, dividends and profits received from the rest of the world minus those paid out. GDP is about location; GNI is about ownership. The World Bank uses GNI per capita to classify countries by income. India's GNI is slightly below its GDP because it pays more interest, dividends and profits to foreign investors than it receives. Ireland's GDP far exceeds its GNI because multinationals book profits there, so Ireland also publishes a modified measure, GNI*. Common confusion: most remittances from migrant workers are treated as current transfers, not factor income, so they largely fall outside GNI.
example: Say an economy's GDP is ₹300 lakh crore. Its residents earn ₹4 lakh crore in interest, dividends and wages from abroad and pay ₹7 lakh crore to foreign investors and workers. GNI = 300 + 4 - 7 = ₹297 lakh crore.
formula: GNP (GNI) = GDP + Factor income received from abroad - Factor income paid abroad

short: Total spending by households and the non-profits serving them on goods and services such as food, rent, clothes, transport and phones.
kid: It is everything all the families in the country buy in a year: food, toys, bus rides and haircuts, added together.
detail: Private final consumption expenditure is the C in GDP = C + I + G + (X - M): purchases by households and the non-profit institutions serving them, including the imputed rent of people living in their own homes. Buying a new house is excluded, because it counts as investment. PFCE is the largest part of India's GDP, close to 60% at current prices in the years up to 2025, against nearly 70% in the United States, so household demand is the main engine of growth. For investors, PFCE growth drives revenues in FMCG, autos, retail, consumer durables and retail lending; analysts track it alongside two-wheeler sales, GST collections and rural wages. Common confusion: PFCE is not the same as retail sales, which capture mainly goods sold in shops; PFCE also covers services such as health, education, transport and rent.
example: Say households spend ₹170 lakh crore in an economy with GDP of ₹300 lakh crore. The PFCE share is 170 / 300 = about 56.7%. If PFCE grows 8% next year, consumption rises by ₹13.6 lakh crore to ₹183.6 lakh crore.
formula: PFCE share of GDP (%) = PFCE / GDP x 100

short: An economy's spending on long-lasting assets such as factories, machinery, roads, homes and software, before allowing for wear and tear.
kid: When a lemonade stand buys a new table and a big jug that will last for years, it is building for the future. This adds up all such buys in the whole country.
detail: Gross fixed capital formation is the investment part of GDP excluding changes in inventories and valuables. It covers private and public spending on buildings, infrastructure, machinery, vehicles and intellectual property such as software and research. Gross means depreciation has not been deducted. The ratio of GFCF to GDP, often called the investment rate, shows how much an economy is building future capacity; India's was roughly 30% of GDP in the years up to 2025, below its highs of the late 2000s and early 2010s. Markets watch it as a gauge of the capex cycle, which drives orders for capital goods, cement, steel and infrastructure companies, and demand for bank credit. Common confusion: GFCF is investment in physical and intangible assets, not buying shares or mutual funds, which are financial investments. A household buying a newly built home does count.
example: Say an economy with GDP of ₹300 lakh crore invests ₹54 lakh crore in buildings and roads, ₹30 lakh crore in machinery and ₹6 lakh crore in software and research. GFCF = 54 + 30 + 6 = ₹90 lakh crore, an investment rate of 90 / 300 = 30%.
formula: Investment rate (%) = GFCF / GDP x 100

short: The value of a country's exports of goods and services minus the value of its imports; negative means it imports more than it sells abroad.
kid: If you give your friends 5 cookies and they give you 8, you got 3 more than you gave. A country keeps the same kind of count with other countries.
detail: Net exports are the (X - M) term in GDP. Imports are subtracted because their value is already included in consumption, investment and government spending but was not produced at home. When net exports are negative, the country runs a trade deficit and the external sector subtracts from the level of GDP. India usually has negative net exports: a large goods deficit, driven by crude oil, electronics and gold, outweighs its surplus in services such as IT and business services. What moves GDP growth is the change in net exports, so a shrinking deficit adds to growth even while net exports stay negative. For markets, net exports depend on the exchange rate and global demand, and feed into the current account and the rupee. Common confusion: a trade deficit is not automatically bad; it can reflect strong domestic investment financed by foreign capital.
example: Say a country exports goods and services worth ₹75 lakh crore and imports ₹85 lakh crore. Net exports are 75 - 85 = minus ₹10 lakh crore. If exports rise to ₹80 lakh crore next year while imports stay at ₹85 lakh crore, net exports improve to minus ₹5 lakh crore, adding ₹5 lakh crore to GDP, all else equal.
formula: Net exports = Exports - Imports

short: The total amount of goods and services that households, firms, government and foreign buyers want to buy in an economy at a given price level.
kid: Think of everyone in town who wants lemonade, toys and bus rides, all added together. When lots of people want lots of things, the shops get very busy.
detail: Aggregate demand is total planned spending in an economy: consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports. Plotted against the overall price level, the AD curve slopes down, because higher prices reduce real wealth, push up interest rates and make exports less competitive. The curve shifts when spending changes for other reasons: rate cuts, tax cuts, higher government capex, rising confidence or stronger exports shift it right; rate hikes or fiscal tightening shift it left. Central banks manage aggregate demand with interest rates, and governments with budgets, to keep it in line with the economy's capacity. Too much demand relative to supply fuels inflation; too little leaves factories idle and costs jobs. Common confusion: a movement along the AD curve, caused by a change in prices, is different from a shift of the whole curve, caused by a change in spending at every price level.
example: Say households plan to spend ₹170 lakh crore, firms invest ₹95 lakh crore, the government spends ₹35 lakh crore and net exports are minus ₹10 lakh crore. Aggregate demand = 170 + 95 + 35 - 10 = ₹290 lakh crore. If the economy can comfortably produce only ₹285 lakh crore, the ₹5 lakh crore of excess demand tends to push prices up.
formula: AD = C + I + G + (X - M)

short: The total amount of goods and services that all firms in an economy are willing and able to produce at each overall price level.
kid: It is how many cakes, toys and bikes all the shops and workshops in town can make. With more helpers and better tools, they can make more.
detail: Aggregate supply links an economy's total output to its price level. In the short run (SRAS) the curve slopes upward: wages and some prices are slow to adjust, so firms produce more when selling prices rise. In the long run (LRAS) the curve is vertical at potential output, which is set by labour, capital, technology and institutions rather than by prices. Supply shocks shift SRAS: a jump in crude oil prices, a weak monsoon or supply-chain disruption shifts it left, raising prices and cutting output together, while cheaper energy or productivity gains shift it right. Better infrastructure, skills and reforms shift LRAS right. For investors, supply shocks are awkward because they push inflation up as growth slows, limiting what central banks can do. Common confusion: aggregate supply is economy-wide, not the supply curve of a single market.
example: Say an economy produces ₹300 lakh crore of output at potential. An oil shock raises costs and firms cut output by 2% to ₹294 lakh crore while prices rise. When new roads and power plants later lift potential output by 3%, the long-run supply curve shifts right to ₹309 lakh crore.

short: The highest level of output an economy can sustain over time with its workers, machines and technology without pushing inflation up.
kid: A runner can sprint very fast for a short while but then gets tired. This is the speed the runner can keep up all day without getting worn out.
detail: Potential output is the level of real GDP an economy can produce when labour and capital are used at normal, sustainable rates. It is not the absolute maximum: an economy can run above potential for a while, but doing so tends to create inflation. Potential growth depends on growth in the workforce, investment in capital and productivity. It cannot be observed directly, so central banks and bodies such as the IMF estimate it with statistical filters and production-function models, and the estimates are revised often. Estimates of India's potential growth by the RBI and others differ and change as new data arrive, so check the latest work rather than treating any figure as fixed. For investors, potential growth sets the long-run ceiling for real earnings growth and helps judge whether policy rates are restrictive. Common confusion: very fast growth after a slump is often recovery, not a rise in potential.
example: Say labour force growth adds 1 percentage point, capital investment adds 3 points and productivity adds 2.5 points. Potential growth is about 1 + 3 + 2.5 = 6.5%. If the economy starts at potential and actual growth runs at 8% for two years, output ends up about 2.8% above potential (1.08 x 1.08 / (1.065 x 1.065) - 1), and inflation pressure tends to build.
formula: Potential growth ≈ Contribution of labour + Contribution of capital + Productivity growth

short: The difference between an economy's actual output and its potential output, usually shown as a percentage of potential.
kid: A lemonade stand can easily make 10 cups a day. If it makes only 8, it has room to do more; if it rushes to make 12, everyone gets tired and grumpy.
detail: The output gap measures how far real GDP is from potential output. A negative gap means the economy is producing below capacity, with idle factories, weak hiring and soft pricing power, which tends to pull inflation down. A positive gap means demand is running ahead of sustainable supply, which tends to push inflation up. Central banks, including the RBI, weigh the gap when deciding how much to tighten or ease; a negative gap supports lower rates if inflation allows. Because potential output is estimated rather than observed, the gap is uncertain and often revised, sometimes even changing sign later. For investors, a negative gap that is closing usually means improving earnings and less room for further rate cuts. Common confusion: a negative output gap does not mean the economy is shrinking; it can grow quickly and still be below potential.
example: Say potential output is ₹300 lakh crore and actual real GDP is ₹294 lakh crore. The output gap is (294 - 300) / 300 x 100 = minus 2%. If actual GDP rises to ₹306 lakh crore while potential stays at ₹300 lakh crore, the gap becomes plus 2%.
formula: Output gap (%) = (Actual GDP - Potential GDP) / Potential GDP x 100

short: A general, sustained rise in the prices of goods and services, which means each rupee buys a little less over time.
kid: Last year one coin bought you a big lollipop. This year the same coin buys only a smaller one, because things slowly cost more.
detail: Inflation is the rate at which the overall price level rises, usually measured as the year-on-year change in a price index. In India the headline measure is CPI inflation, released monthly by the National Statistics Office; under the framework as of 2025, the RBI targets 4% CPI inflation with a tolerance band of 2-6%. The US Federal Reserve targets 2% on the PCE price index. Moderate, stable inflation is normal in a growing economy. High or volatile inflation erodes savings and real wages and pushes central banks to raise rates, which hurts bond prices and equity valuations. Investors therefore focus on real returns: nominal return minus inflation. Common confusions: one item getting dearer is not inflation; falling inflation does not mean falling prices (that is deflation); and the inflation rate is a change, not a price level.
example: Say the CPI is 200.0 in March this year and 192.0 in March last year. Inflation = (200.0 / 192.0 - 1) x 100 = about 4.2%. A deposit paying 7% then earns a real return of roughly 7 - 4.2 = 2.8%.
formula: Inflation (%) = (Price index this period / Price index a year earlier - 1) x 100

short: An index that tracks the average change in prices households pay for a fixed basket of goods and services, used to measure retail inflation.
kid: Imagine a shopping bag with milk, rice, a bus ticket and a haircut inside. Each year we check how much more the very same bag costs.
detail: The Consumer Price Index measures the cost of a representative basket of household purchases, such as food, fuel, clothing, housing, transport, health and education, relative to a base period set at 100. Each item is weighted by its share in household spending surveys. In India, the National Statistics Office under MoSPI releases CPI for rural, urban and combined India around the 12th of each month; combined CPI inflation is the measure the RBI targets. The base year and weights are revised periodically to reflect changing spending, which has tended to lower the weight of food over time. In the US, the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes the CPI. A print above expectations can push bond yields up and reduce rate-cut hopes. Common confusion: the CPI is a price level; CPI inflation is the percentage change in it, usually against the same month a year earlier.
example: Say a basket costs ₹10,000 in the base year, so the index is 100. If the same basket costs ₹19,500 today, the CPI is 195.0. If it was 187.5 a year ago, CPI inflation is 195.0 / 187.5 - 1 = 4.0%.
formula: CPI = (Cost of basket today / Cost of basket in base year) x 100

short: An index of the prices domestic producers receive for their output, tracking inflation at the factory gate before goods reach shops.
kid: Before toys reach the shop, the toy maker sells them to the shopkeeper. This checks whether the toy maker is asking for more than last year.
detail: A Producer Price Index measures the average change in selling prices received by domestic producers for goods and, in many countries, services. Sub-indices are published by stage of production, from raw materials through intermediate goods to finished goods, so they can signal cost pressures before they reach consumers. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics releases a monthly PPI, and China's PPI is watched as a gauge of global goods prices; it spent long stretches in deflation in the 2010s and again from late 2022. India has long relied on the Wholesale Price Index instead, with a PPI under development, as of 2025, to replace it. For investors, rising producer prices can squeeze margins of companies that buy those goods, or foreshadow higher consumer inflation if costs are passed on. Common confusion: PPI excludes sales taxes and retail markups, so it can diverge sharply from consumer inflation.
example: Say the producer price index for steel is 140.0 this month and 133.0 a year ago. Steel PPI inflation = (140.0 / 133.0 - 1) x 100 = about 5.3%. If a hypothetical steel-using carmaker, say ABC Motors Ltd, raised its car prices only 2% over the same year, its margins are being squeezed.
formula: PPI inflation (%) = (PPI this period / PPI a year earlier - 1) x 100

short: A US price index, published by the Bureau of Economic Analysis, that measures inflation in household spending; the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge.
kid: In America, someone checks how much more families pay each year for food, doctor visits and everything else. The people in charge of America's money watch this check most closely.
detail: The PCE price index is compiled monthly by the US Bureau of Economic Analysis from the personal consumption expenditures component of GDP. The Federal Reserve defines its 2% inflation goal in terms of annual PCE inflation and pays close attention to core PCE, which excludes volatile food and energy prices. PCE inflation usually runs a few tenths of a percentage point below CPI inflation because it covers a broader range of spending, including healthcare paid by employers and government on households' behalf, gives housing a smaller weight, and uses a chain-weighted formula that captures consumers switching to cheaper goods. Because CPI and PPI data come out earlier in the month, economists can forecast PCE closely, so surprises tend to be small. For Indian investors, US core PCE matters because it shapes Fed rate decisions, which move the dollar, US Treasury yields and foreign flows into Indian markets.
example: Say the core PCE price index is 125.6 this month and 122.0 a year ago. Core PCE inflation = (125.6 / 122.0 - 1) x 100 = about 2.95%, nearly a percentage point above the Fed's 2% goal. If CPI inflation in the same month were 3.3%, PCE would be running about 0.35 points below it.
formula: PCE inflation (%) = (PCE price index this month / PCE price index a year earlier - 1) x 100

short: The inflation rate for the full consumer basket, including volatile items such as food and fuel, as reported in the monthly release.
kid: It is the big number for how much more everything in the shopping bag costs, including fruit and vegetables whose prices jump up and down a lot.
detail: Headline inflation is the year-on-year change in the full Consumer Price Index, with nothing excluded. It is the number in newspaper headlines and, in India, the measure on which the RBI's inflation target is set, so it directly shapes policy-rate decisions. Because it includes food and energy, headline inflation can swing sharply with the monsoon, vegetable prices such as tomatoes and onions, or crude oil. Central banks therefore also study core inflation to judge the underlying trend, but they cannot ignore headline for long, since it is what households feel and it drives inflation expectations. A big headline surprise can move bond yields and the rupee within minutes of the release. Common confusions: in India, headline inflation means CPI inflation, not WPI inflation, and a fall driven only by food prices or a base effect can reverse within months.
example: Say food prices rise 8% with a 40% weight in the basket, fuel rises 2% with a 7% weight and everything else rises 4% with a 53% weight. Headline inflation = 0.40 x 8 + 0.07 x 2 + 0.53 x 4 = 3.2 + 0.14 + 2.12 = 5.46%, while inflation excluding food and fuel is 4%.
formula: Headline inflation = Sum of (item weight x item inflation) across the full CPI basket

short: Inflation measured after removing volatile items, usually food and energy, to show the underlying trend in prices.
kid: Some fruits cost more one week and less the next, which is confusing. If we leave out the jumpy things, we can see how prices are really moving.
detail: Core inflation strips the most volatile components out of a price index so policymakers can see the persistent trend. In the US, core CPI and core PCE exclude food and energy. India has no single official core series: analysts, and the RBI in its reports, usually compute CPI excluding food and beverages and fuel and light, and sometimes also petrol, diesel, gold and silver, since precious metal prices can distort it. Core inflation reflects demand conditions, wages and services prices, so it moves slowly and is often a better guide to future headline inflation than one month's headline print. Central banks watch it to judge whether a supply shock is spreading into broader prices. Common confusion: excluding food does not mean food prices do not matter; in India food is a large share of household spending, and persistent food shocks can feed into wages and core over time.
example: Say headline CPI inflation is 5.5% because vegetable prices jumped, while CPI excluding food and fuel rose 3.8%. Core inflation is 3.8%, suggesting the underlying trend is near a 4% target and the food spike may fade. If core had instead risen from 3.8% to 4.8%, the price pressure would look broad-based.
formula: Core inflation = Inflation in the price index excluding food and energy (food and fuel in India)

short: The rate at which prices of food items such as cereals, pulses, vegetables, milk and edible oils rise over a year.
kid: When the same basket of rice, vegetables and milk costs more than it did a year ago, food has become dearer. Too much or too little rain can make vegetables cost more.
detail: Food inflation is the year-on-year change in food prices within a consumer price index. In India, the National Statistics Office publishes the Consumer Food Price Index (CFPI) alongside the CPI. Food carries a large weight in India's CPI, close to half for food and beverages in the 2012-base series, and base revisions tend to lower it, so food swings often decide the headline number. Prices are driven by the monsoon, heatwaves, crop disease, global edible oil and grain prices, government stocks, export curbs and minimum support prices; tomato, onion and potato prices can swing sharply. The RBI usually looks through short-lived food spikes, but persistent food inflation can lift inflation expectations and wages. For markets, high food inflation squeezes rural and lower-income spending and can delay rate cuts. Common confusion: CFPI covers food items only, a narrower group than food and beverages, which also includes prepared meals and drinks.
example: Say a family's monthly food basket cost ₹8,000 a year ago and costs ₹8,640 today. Food inflation for that family is 640 / 8,000 = 8%. If food carries a 40% weight in the CPI, it alone adds 0.40 x 8 = 3.2 percentage points to headline inflation.
formula: Food inflation (%) = (Food price index this month / Food price index a year earlier - 1) x 100

short: Inflation that stays high and comes down only slowly, usually because services prices, wages and rents adjust gradually.
kid: Some prices are like chewing gum stuck to a shoe: once they go up, they are very hard to pull back down.
detail: Sticky inflation describes price rises that persist even after the original shock has faded or policy has tightened. It usually comes from items that are repriced slowly, such as rents, wages, insurance, education, healthcare and other services, where contracts and price lists change only once or twice a year. The Atlanta Fed publishes a sticky-price CPI built from such items. After the 2021-22 surge, inflation in the US and Europe fell quickly as goods and energy prices eased, but the last mile back to 2% proved slow because services inflation stayed sticky. For markets, sticky inflation means central banks keep rates higher for longer, pushing back expected rate cuts and weighing on bonds and richly valued stocks. Common confusion: sticky prices in economic theory means individual prices are slow to change; sticky inflation is the economy-wide result, an inflation rate that is slow to fall.
example: Say goods inflation falls from 8% to 2% within a year while services inflation only eases from 6% to 5%. With services at 60% of the basket, overall inflation drops from 0.4 x 8 + 0.6 x 6 = 6.8% to 0.4 x 2 + 0.6 x 5 = 3.8%, and stays stuck there until services cool.

short: What households, firms and investors believe inflation will be in future, which shapes wage demands, pricing and interest rates today.
kid: If everyone thinks sweets will cost more next month, the shop asks for more coins and children ask for more pocket money. Just expecting it can help make it happen.
detail: Inflation expectations are beliefs about future price rises. They matter because they feed into actual inflation: workers seek higher wages, firms raise prices in advance and lenders demand higher interest rates. Expectations are anchored when people trust the central bank to keep inflation near target despite temporary shocks, and de-anchored when they rise with each shock, which forces much tougher policy, as in the 1970s. They are measured through surveys, such as the RBI's bi-monthly Inflation Expectations Survey of Households and the University of Michigan survey in the US, and through markets, such as breakeven inflation, the gap between nominal and inflation-indexed bond yields. Much of central bank communication aims to keep expectations anchored. Common confusion: household surveys in India usually show expectations well above actual inflation, so analysts watch their direction more than their level.
example: Say a 10-year government bond yields 7.0% and an inflation-indexed bond of the same maturity yields 2.8%. Breakeven inflation is 7.0 - 2.8 = 4.2%, meaning investors expect about 4.2% inflation a year on average. If the gap widens to 5.2%, expectations are drifting up.
formula: Breakeven inflation ≈ Nominal bond yield - Inflation-indexed bond yield

short: Inflation caused when total spending in an economy grows faster than the economy's ability to produce goods and services.
kid: If ten children all want the last five ice creams, the seller can ask for more. Too many people wanting the same things makes them cost more.
detail: Demand-pull inflation happens when aggregate demand outruns aggregate supply: too much money chasing too few goods. Sources include rapid credit growth, large fiscal stimulus, very low interest rates, an export boom or soaring asset prices that make people feel richer. With factories and workers already near full use, firms meet extra orders by raising prices rather than output, and tight labour markets push wages up. The US in 2021-22 is a recent case, when stimulus payments and pent-up demand met constrained supply. The usual cure is demand management: raising policy rates and tightening fiscal policy to cool spending. For investors, demand-pull inflation often comes with strong growth and earnings at first, but the higher rates that follow eventually weigh on valuations. Common confusion: it differs from cost-push inflation, where rising costs rather than excess demand drive prices up.
example: Say an economy can produce ₹300 lakh crore of goods and services, but stimulus lifts planned spending to ₹312 lakh crore. Demand exceeds capacity by 12 / 300 = 4%, so firms raise prices rather than output. A central bank might respond by raising rates to bring spending back towards ₹300 lakh crore.

short: Inflation caused by rising production costs, such as fuel, raw materials or wages, that firms pass on to buyers as higher prices.
kid: If sugar and lemons suddenly cost more, the lemonade stand has to ask for more coins per cup, even though no extra people want lemonade.
detail: Cost-push inflation starts on the supply side. When inputs become dearer, through an oil price spike, a poor harvest, a weaker currency that raises import costs, supply-chain bottlenecks or sharp wage increases, firms raise selling prices to protect margins. Unlike demand-pull inflation, it often comes with slower growth, because higher costs reduce output; the 1970s oil shocks are the textbook case. For India, imported crude oil and edible oils plus monsoon-driven food prices make cost-push episodes common. It creates a dilemma for central banks: raising rates does little to fix supply and hurts growth further, but ignoring it risks a wage-price spiral if expectations rise. For investors, companies with pricing power fare better, while those that cannot pass on costs see margins shrink. Common confusion: a one-time cost jump raises the price level once; it becomes lasting inflation only if it feeds into wages and expectations.
example: Say a hypothetical firm, ABC Paints Ltd, makes a tin of paint for ₹400, of which crude-linked chemicals cost ₹160. If chemical prices rise 25%, costs go up by ₹40 to ₹440, a 10% rise. To keep the same 20% profit margin, ABC must raise the tin's price by 10%, from ₹500 to ₹550.

short: A sustained fall in the general price level, meaning the inflation rate is below zero and money buys more over time.
kid: If your coin buys one lollipop today and two lollipops next year, prices are falling. That sounds nice, but people may wait to buy, and the shops get very quiet.
detail: Deflation is negative inflation: the overall price level falls for a sustained period, not just a few items. It may sound good for buyers, but broad deflation usually signals weak demand and can feed on itself. People delay purchases expecting lower prices, firms cut output and wages, and the real burden of debt rises because incomes fall while loan amounts do not. Central banks find it hard to fight because policy rates cannot go far below zero. The US suffered severe deflation in the Great Depression, with consumer prices falling about a quarter between 1929 and 1933, and Japan struggled with mild deflation for long periods from the late 1990s into the 2010s. For investors, deflation tends to favour high-quality government bonds and hurt equities and commodities. Common confusion: inflation falling from 6% to 3% is disinflation, not deflation; prices are still rising.
example: Say a price index falls from 100.0 to 98.0 over a year, deflation of 2%. A borrower paying 5% interest on a ₹10 lakh loan faces a real interest rate of about 5 - (-2) = 7%, and if wages also fall 2%, the same debt takes up a bigger share of income.
formula: Deflation rate (%) = (Price index this year / Price index last year - 1) x 100, when the result is negative

short: A slowdown in the rate of inflation: prices are still rising, but more slowly than before.
kid: Your lollipop used to cost a lot more each year. Now it still costs a bit more, but only a tiny bit more each year.
detail: Disinflation is a fall in the inflation rate while it stays positive, for example from 7% to 4%. The price level keeps rising, only at a slower pace. It is usually the goal after an inflation surge and typically comes from tighter monetary policy, easing supply shocks, falling commodity prices or a favourable base effect. The global disinflation of 2023-24, after inflation peaked in 2022, is a recent example: goods prices cooled quickly, services more slowly. Markets welcome disinflation because it opens the door to rate cuts, which tend to lift bond prices and support equity valuations. Historically, though, bringing inflation down without a recession has been hard, so investors watch growth alongside it. Common confusion: disinflation is not deflation; shoppers do not see prices fall, they see them rise more gently, which is why many people feel little relief.
example: Say the CPI rises from 100 to 107 in year one (7% inflation) and from 107 to 111.28 in year two. Inflation in year two is 111.28 / 107 - 1 = 4%, so inflation fell from 7% to 4%, yet prices are 11.28% higher than two years earlier.

short: A policy-driven recovery of growth and inflation after a slump or deflation; also an investment strategy betting on that recovery.
kid: After a long, sleepy winter, the town tries to wake up and get busy again. People start shopping and building, and prices slowly start rising like before.
detail: Reflation describes efforts, through rate cuts, central bank money creation or government spending, to pull an economy out of a downturn and lift inflation back towards a normal level after a period of weak or falling prices. The term is also used for the early recovery phase when growth and inflation both pick up. In markets, the reflation trade means positioning for that shift: buying cyclical sectors such as banks, metals, energy and industrials, plus commodities and small caps, while selling long-dated government bonds because yields tend to rise and the yield curve steepens. Notable episodes include the months after the November 2016 US election and the vaccine-led recovery of late 2020 and 2021. Common confusion: reflation is not simply inflation; it means bringing prices and activity back to a healthy trend from a depressed level, and the trade can reverse quickly if growth disappoints.
example: Say a country has had 0% inflation and 1% growth. After rate cuts and a $500 billion spending package, growth rises to 4% and inflation to 2%. An investor running a reflation trade buys bank and metal stocks and sells long-term bonds; if the 10-year yield rises from 1.0% to 1.8%, bond prices fall, so the short bond position gains.

short: A painful mix of high inflation, weak or falling economic growth and rising unemployment, all happening at the same time.
kid: Imagine the shops are quiet, many grown-ups cannot find work, and yet sweets keep costing more. It is a sad mix of two problems at once.
detail: Stagflation combines stagnation, meaning slow or negative growth and high unemployment, with high inflation. It usually follows a large supply shock, such as an oil price jump, that raises costs and cuts output at the same time. The 1970s are the classic case: after the 1973 and 1979 oil shocks, the US, UK and other economies saw double-digit inflation alongside recessions, breaking the belief that inflation and unemployment always move in opposite directions. Stagflation is a nightmare for central banks, since raising rates to fight inflation deepens the slowdown, while cutting rates to support growth risks entrenching inflation. It is hard on portfolios too: stocks and conventional bonds can fall together, while commodities and inflation-protected assets have historically held up better. Common confusion: one weak quarter with high inflation is not stagflation; the term implies a persistent combination.
example: In 1974, US consumer prices rose about 11% while real GDP shrank slightly, and unemployment climbed to about 9% by mid-1975. In such a year, a portfolio earning a 10% nominal return against 11% inflation loses about 1% of its purchasing power (1.10 / 1.11 - 1 = about -0.9%).
